experiment.name: Human-to-dog mechanism transfer grid: severity mechanisms from malaria, human babesiosis and sepsis that are unmeasured in canine babesiosis
experiment.description: Which mechanisms linked to severity in malaria, human babesiosis and sepsis have not been measured against severity in dogs with babesiosis, have a canine assay, and could be tested now? Premise: most mechanisms with good human evidence are unmeasured in dogs.

parameters.note: No outcomes file opened; no statistical test.

experiment.summary: 37 mechanisms in 7 families: 21 are gaps (no canine severity data; 12 never measured in dogs with babesiosis), 16 already tested against severity. 21 of 36 mechanisms with human grade 2 or 3 are gaps; 21 meet the ranking rule; of the top 10, 2 have a protein in the DS07 proteome. No statistical tests.

ranked.mechanism: Calprotectin (S100A8/A9) and S100A12 as circulating neutrophil activation alarmins
Neutrophil extracellular traps (cell-free DNA, MPO-DNA, citrullinated histone H3)
Released (plasma) myeloperoxidase and neutrophil elastase, as degranulation markers distinct from the cellular MPXI
VWF antigen, ultra-large multimers and ADAMTS13 (ratio)

eligible_not_ranked: Regulatory T cells and T-cell exhaustion (PD-1, PD-L1)
Monocyte deactivation (HLA-DR / DLA class II expression)
Soluble endothelial protein C receptor (sEPCR) shedding
ADMA and arginine bioavailability (plasma arginine:ADMA ratio)

ranked.human_direction: Ang-2 and the Ang-2/Ang-1 ratio are higher in severe and fatal malaria (falciparum, knowlesi, vivax) and in sepsis non-survivors and sepsis AKI. Ang-1 is lower.

sFlt-1 (soluble VEGFR-1) is higher in sepsis with ARDS and in non-survivors (a systematic review and meta-analysis supports prognostic value). VEGF results in malaria are mixed: higher in severe vivax malaria, but proposed as protective in cerebral malaria.

ranked.mechanism: Neutrophil extracellular traps (cell-free DNA, MPO-DNA, citrullinated histone H3)
ranked.human_direction: higher in severe or fatal disease: cfDNA rises from uncomplicated to cerebral malaria and separates fatal retinopathy-positive cases; NET counts, elastase and CitH3 rise with severity in falciparum and knowlesi malaria; sepsis meta-analyses report higher cfDNA in non-survivors. Counterpoint: in HU008 (341 ICU patients) cfDNA and MPO-DNA did not predict death after severity adjustment; only an ex vivo NET-induction assay did.

higher with severity and death: in paediatric cerebral malaria circulating histones are raised, roughly half of parasite origin, and track brain swelling; in 420 ICU patients histone levels correlate with organ injury markers and SOFA; in two smaller sepsis cohorts histones are far higher in non-survivors

ranked.mechanism: Calprotectin (S100A8/A9) and S100A12 as circulating neutrophil activation alarmins
ranked.human_direction: higher with severity: a 21-cohort meta-analysis gives a pooled prognostic AUC of about 0.74 for circulating calprotectin in acute infection and sepsis; single cohorts link it to hospital mortality independently of renal function and to sepsis-associated AKI; S100A8/A9 genes sit in the neutrophil granule signature of severe malaria. Effects are moderate and calprotectin did not beat clinical severity scores.

ranked.mechanism: VWF antigen, ultra-large multimers and ADAMTS13 (ratio)
ranked.human_direction: VWF antigen, VWF activity and ultra-large multimers higher in severe and cerebral malaria; ADAMTS13 activity lower, so the VWF/ADAMTS13 ratio is higher in severe disease

higher in fatal sepsis/septic shock (MIMIC-IV n=718, OR 1.97 above 526 ng/mL; paediatric cohorts n=115 and n=123; septic shock n=79, https://doi.org/10.7759/cureus.115711); in malaria, ferritin is much higher in clinical than in asymptomatic infection (meta-analysis), but it is not independent of SOFA in some cohorts

higher IDO activity (kynurenine:tryptophan) and kynurenine with sepsis severity and death; CSF kynurenine and kynurenic acid with longer coma in cerebral malaria; kynurenine is vasodilatory and lowers blood pressure in murine malaria

ranked.mechanism: Released (plasma) myeloperoxidase and neutrophil elastase, as degranulation markers distinct from the cellular MPXI
ranked.human_direction: higher in severe disease: plasma elastase and MPO raised in retinopathy-positive cerebral malaria, soluble elastase rises with severity and with acute lung injury in knowlesi malaria, plasma MPO correlates with cfDNA in fatal paediatric cerebral malaria, neutrophil degranulation genes raised in sepsis non-survivors

plasma HO-1 higher in severe malaria (Gambian children) and higher HO-1 linked to death in cerebral malaria (Ugandan children); HMOX1 promoter repeat linked to severe disease/death; serum HO-1 higher in septic AKI

rows.agent_summary: Every upstream step of the haem scavenging chain is a gap in canine babesiosis: cfHb, haemopexin and haptoglobin have been measured only against controls or over time, and HO-1 and ADMA never; all have grade 2-3 human severity evidence and a canine assay, and cfHb (DS02, DS07 HBB), HMOX1 and HPX (DS06) are in public files. Not gaps: NO metabolites (Jacobson 2002, no severity signal) and the downstream lipid peroxidation readout (MDA, 3 severity-tested units). Surprise: both canine proteomic studies report haemopexin raised, not depleted, in infected dogs; haptoglobin findings are inconsistent (low, normal, raised).

Angiopoietin-2, glycocalyx shedding (syndecan-1, hyaluronan, heparan sulfate) and VEGF/sFlt-1 have never been measured in dogs with babesiosis (PubMed and local corpus, 2026-11-12). All three have strong human severity evidence: malaria cohorts plus sepsis meta-analyses. All three also have canine assays already used in canine sepsis or critical care, so they are true gaps. Soluble adhesion molecules are not a gap: CB004 (Zagreb, B. canis) compared sICAM-1 and sVCAM-1 between complicated and uncomplicated dogs, and only VCAM-1 differed at admission. Surprise: the canine Ang-2 data come from validated cross-reactive human ELISAs, and Ang-2 was higher in septic non-survivors. But ANGPT2 itself is not among the DS06 genes (only ANGPT1 and TEK), and no F2 protein is a DS07 master protein.

NETs (cfDNA, nucleosomes, MPO-DNA, CitH3) and circulating extracellular histones are grade-3 human severity mechanisms in malaria and sepsis, have canine assays already used in sepsis, IMHA, heatstroke and pancreatitis, and have never been measured in dogs with babesiosis: both are clear gaps. The granule-protein seed row is only partly filled in dogs: MPXI is an intracellular analyser index and NGAL studies are renal, so released plasma MPO/elastase and calprotectin/S100A12 are split out as added rows and are also gaps. DS07 (CB112 serum proteome, severity-labelled) already carries master proteins for histone H4, S100A8 and lactotransferrin, of which only lactotransferrin was reported.

The only real gap in this family is the VWF/ADAMTS13 axis: one small study (CB446, 12 dogs vs 10 controls) measured VWF in dogs with babesiosis, without a severity contrast, and no study has measured ADAMTS13. Canine assays exist for both (VWF:Ag ELISA, ADAMTS13 activity ELISA), but neither protein is a master protein in DS07, so testing needs stored plasma. Only DS06 has them, as whole-blood gene expression. Fibrinolytic shutdown (PAI-1, alpha-2-antiplasmin) and the anticoagulant pathway (antithrombin, protein C, thrombomodulin) have already been tested against severity: 2 and 4 independent units. Most of the 70 F4-04 keyword hits only mention DIC. Surprises: alpha-2-antiplasmin rose in survivors but not in non-survivors (CB145); PAI-1 and TAFI were low at admission in B. canis, so consumption, not shutdown (CB004); and soluble EPCR (added) was measured once in uncomplicated cases only.

Ferritin is the one clear gap. Human evidence is strong (several sepsis cohorts, including a MIMIC-IV cohort of 718, link high ferritin to death). In dogs with babesiosis, ferritin was measured only in a 7-vs-7 seropositive case-control study (no difference) and in two case reports, and never against severity. A canine-specific ferritin immunoassay is in routine use. Hepcidin and serum iron/transferrin are not gaps, but the evidence is thin: hepcidin rests on one small Indian cohort (CH08, survivors vs non-survivors, probably confounded by species), and iron/transferrin has 4 units (CH08, CH12, CH07, CB112). One surprise: DS07 is the CB112 proteome, so its transferrin rows have already been tested by severity. Another: the local keyword list missed CB073 (CH07, lower iron in SIRS dogs) because that note says only 'iron'. No HU article bears on iron.

Cortisol, thyroid hormones and lactate/hypoglycaemia are NOT gaps: each has 5 to 8 independent canine severity or outcome units (cortisol and T4 mostly Onderstepoort B. rossi: CB040, CH31, CB342, CH09, plus CB486 or CH35 from B. canis; lactate in B. rossi, B. canis and B. gibsoni). The two gaps are the kynurenine pathway (serum kynurenine measured only infected vs healthy in B. canis, CB091; canine LC-MS/MS method validated; IDO1/KMO in DS06, per-dog metabolite tables in public supplements S-CB091/S-CB071) and copeptin/vasopressin (never measured in canine babesiosis; canine ELISA used but its agreement with AVP is doubtful). Of 5 grade >=2 mechanisms, 2 (40%) are gaps. Surprises: adrenal androgens (DHEA) have never been measured in dogs with babesiosis, and the Onderstepoort endocrine units may share patients.

IL-10/TNF is not a gap: 5 independent canine units compared IL-10 or TNF by severity or outcome (CH03, CB037, CH23, CB109, CH37). No dog study reported the IL-10/TNF ratio itself; DS02 has both cytokines. Soluble CD14 (CB112, complicated > uncomplicated, which is DS07 itself) and suPAR (CB004, complicated vs uncomplicated B. canis, no difference) are also already severity-tested. The real gaps are regulatory T cells / PD-1 (never measured in canine babesiosis; CB008 measured only CD3/CD4/CD8/B cells), monocyte DLA class II (only whole-blood transcripts in CB082/DS06), soluble TREM-1 (no canine soluble assay found) and complement factor H (added; only in proteomics, CB019 pools and DS07 master A0A5F4BVG1, never reported by severity). One surprise: the DS07 factor H masters are labelled 'Uncharacterized protein ... GN=CFH', so a description-prefix match on 'Complement factor H' will miss them; match on GN=CFH.

rows.human_direction: higher in severe malaria (falciparum and knowlesi), with AKI and in fatal cases; independently higher in sepsis non-survivors
rows.notes: Jacobson 2002 (B. rossi, mild/severe/complicated groups) used free serum Hb as a covariate for nitric oxide metabolites; the abstract reports no cfHb-by-severity result, so it is not counted. CFH spectrophotometry is used in a canine sepsis model (purpose-bred Beagles), not formally validated. HU022 is brain tissue Hb by near-infrared spectroscopy, tangential.

rows.human_direction: free haem (haemin, labile haem) higher and haemopexin lower in severe and fatal paediatric malaria; in sepsis haemopexin was not independently linked to death and in Angolan children haemopexin was not a risk factor
rows.notes: Surprise: both canine proteomic studies report haemopexin HIGHER in infected dogs, opposite to the human 'depletion' direction. Canine haemopexin has only been quantified by mass spectrometry; no canine immunoassay validation found. Free/labile haem never measured in canine babesiosis.

rows.human_direction: higher haptoglobin independently linked to lower in-hospital mortality in sepsis (effect confined to patients with detectable cfHb); in paediatric malaria haptoglobin was not a risk factor for severe disease
rows.notes: Ulutas 2005 (pre-window) had 6 uncomplicated and 1 complicated dog, so no usable severity contrast. Canine Hp is a positive acute-phase protein, so consumption by cfHb and induction by inflammation pull in opposite directions; canine results are inconsistent (low, normal, raised). Haemolysis lowers measured Hp in the validated canine assay.

rows.human_direction: plasma HO-1 higher in severe malaria (Gambian children) and higher HO-1 linked to death in cerebral malaria (Ugandan children); HMOX1 promoter repeat linked to severe disease/death; serum HO-1 higher in septic AKI
rows.notes: Zero PubMed hits for HO-1 in canine babesiosis. Plasma/splenic HO-1 measured in dogs by capture ELISA in visceral leishmaniasis (no formal canine validation).

rows.mechanism: Nitric oxide scavenging and arginine / ADMA
rows.human_direction: lower endothelial NO bioavailability and lower arginine / arginine:ADMA ratio in severe malaria; cfHb inversely related to NO-dependent vascular function
rows.notes: Severity units: Jacobson 2002 (B. rossi, mild/severe uncomplicated/complicated, not in the review, pre-window): serum NO metabolites did not separate severity or outcome; CH06 urinary arginine vs UPC (weak, renal axis only). NO metabolites are not the human exposure (endothelial NO bioavailability, plasma arginine:ADMA); those are unmeasured in dogs with babesiosis. ADMA split out as F1-11.

rows.mechanism: ADMA and arginine bioavailability (plasma arginine:ADMA ratio)
rows.human_direction: arginine:ADMA ratio lower in severe than non-severe malaria (adults) and low in severe paediatric malaria, inversely related to lactate and angiopoietin-2; ADMA itself higher in adults (linked to mortality in that group's work) but lower in children
rows.notes: SDMA (a renal filtration marker, not the NOS inhibitor) was severity-tested in B. rossi (higher in complicated: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ttbdis.2020.101406) and measured in B. canis (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ttbdis.2018.07.012); ADMA never. Canine ADMA by HPLC was linked to death in acute pancreatitis.

rows.human_direction: plasma F2-isoprostanes higher in fatal falciparum malaria and with AKI needing dialysis; in sepsis isoprostanes lower when cfHb-associated oxidation is blocked (acetaminophen)
rows.notes: Added as a check on the premise: the downstream oxidative-damage readout is already severity-tested in 3 canine units (mixed results), while the upstream haem scavenging chain (cfHb, free haem, haemopexin, haptoglobin, HO-1) is not. F2-isoprostanes never measured in canine babesiosis. CB499 has no DOI in articles.jsonl.

rows.human_direction: Ang-2 and the Ang-2/Ang-1 ratio are higher in severe and fatal malaria (falciparum, knowlesi, vivax) and in sepsis non-survivors and sepsis AKI. Ang-1 is lower.
rows.notes: A human Ang-2 ELISA was validated for canine plasma (Ang-1 ELISA failed). In canine SIRS/sepsis, Ang-2 was higher in non-survivors. Ang-2 has been measured in canine leishmaniosis, but never in babesiosis. The DS06 match is partial (receptor and Ang-1 only), and Ang-2 is stored in endothelial Weibel-Palade bodies, so blood RNA is a weak proxy.

rows.human_direction: Higher urinary glycosaminoglycans and plasma syndecan-1 go with severe and fatal falciparum malaria, and with severity in vivax and knowlesi malaria. A sepsis meta-analysis links syndecan-1 to complications and mortality.
rows.notes: Canine syndecan-1, hyaluronan and heparan sulfate ELISAs have been used in trauma, haemorrhage models, anaesthesia (urinary syndecan-1, https://doi.org/10.1111/jvim.17121) and sepsis or critical illness (HA). No formal canine analytical validation was found, so graded used_in_dogs. Hyaluronan is the same molecule in all species. Blood RNA for SDC1 does not reflect endothelial shedding.

rows.mechanism: Soluble endothelial adhesion molecules (ICAM-1, VCAM-1, E-selectin)
rows.human_direction: sICAM-1 (and sVCAM-1, sE-selectin) are higher in cerebral and severe malaria and go with AKI and mortality in paediatric severe malaria. In knowlesi malaria they correlate with endothelial markers.
rows.notes: One severity-tested unit (CB004, 11 vs 19 dogs): only sVCAM-1 at admission was significant. The sICAM-1 direction against controls conflicts between CB384 (lower) and CB446 (higher). No study of sE-selectin in canine babesiosis was found; it remains unmeasured but is folded into this row. Graded validated because canine-specific ELISA kits were used. CB384 has no DOI in the corpus.

rows.human_direction: sFlt-1 (soluble VEGFR-1) is higher in sepsis with ARDS and in non-survivors (a systematic review and meta-analysis supports prognostic value). VEGF results in malaria are mixed: higher in severe vivax malaria, but proposed as protective in cerebral malaria.
rows.notes: The 'validated' grade applies to VEGF only: an ELISA was validated for canine VEGF, and VEGF was higher in septic and non-surviving dogs. No canine sFlt-1 measurement was found. The human grade rests mostly on sepsis sFlt-1; the malaria VEGF evidence is small and inconsistent.

rows.mechanism: Neutrophil extracellular traps (cell-free DNA, MPO-DNA, citrullinated histone H3)
rows.human_direction: higher in severe or fatal disease: cfDNA rises from uncomplicated to cerebral malaria and separates fatal retinopathy-positive cases; NET counts, elastase and CitH3 rise with severity in falciparum and knowlesi malaria; sepsis meta-analyses report higher cfDNA in non-survivors. Counterpoint: in HU008 (341 ICU patients) cfDNA and MPO-DNA did not predict death after severity adjustment; only an ex vivo NET-induction assay did.
rows.notes: Canine cfDNA fluorometry is linear and repeatable and is prognostic in canine sepsis (cfDNA per neutrophil higher in non-survivors, https://doi.org/10.1111/vec.12773); nucleosome ELISA (Nu.Q H3.1) and a histone-DNA ELISA have been evaluated in dogs. Haemolysis and icterus interfere with the nucleosome ELISA (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.vetimm.2015.10.014), a real limitation in haemolytic babesiosis. A dog cfDNA sequencing study (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ygeno.2018.05.020) detected Babesia DNA, not host NETs.

rows.human_direction: higher with severity and death: in paediatric cerebral malaria circulating histones are raised, roughly half of parasite origin, and track brain swelling; in 420 ICU patients histone levels correlate with organ injury markers and SOFA; in two smaller sepsis cohorts histones are far higher in non-survivors
rows.notes: Serum histones have been measured in dogs by ELISA in heatstroke (associated with severity) and in acute pancreatitis, and nucleosome assays in canine cancer, so a canine method exists. Parasite-derived histones are plausible in Babesia (CB010 secretome) but untested in dog blood, and host versus parasite origin would need species-distinguishing peptides, as in the human cerebral malaria work.

rows.mechanism: Neutrophil granule proteins (MPO, elastase, lactoferrin, NGAL, S100A8/A9)
rows.human_direction: higher in severe disease: plasma elastase, MPO and proteinase 3 raised in retinopathy-positive cerebral malaria (lactoferrin and lipocalin were not), neutrophil granule transcripts raised in sepsis non-survivors and in all severe malaria phenotypes in dual RNA-seq, NGAL predicts malarial acute kidney injury
rows.notes: Counted units: CH03 (CB050), CB112, CB053 and CH06/CB103; CB124 adds a fifth but mixes leptospirosis and reports no babesiosis-only severity contrast, so it is not counted. The row is only nominally covered: NGAL is partly a renal tubular marker rather than a neutrophil activation marker, MPXI is cellular not released, and no study measured plasma MPO, elastase or calprotectin. See the two added rows.

rows.mechanism: Released (plasma) myeloperoxidase and neutrophil elastase, as degranulation markers distinct from the cellular MPXI
rows.human_direction: higher in severe disease: plasma elastase and MPO raised in retinopathy-positive cerebral malaria, soluble elastase rises with severity and with acute lung injury in knowlesi malaria, plasma MPO correlates with cfDNA in fatal paediatric cerebral malaria, neutrophil degranulation genes raised in sepsis non-survivors
rows.notes: Split from F3-03 because the only canine babesiosis MPO measure (CB050 MPXI) estimates granule content inside neutrophils and would be expected to move opposite to released MPO. The canine NE ELISA has modest spiking recovery (27 to 114 percent), so analytical validation in haemolysed serum would be needed first.

rows.mechanism: Calprotectin (S100A8/A9) and S100A12 as circulating neutrophil activation alarmins
rows.human_direction: higher with severity: a 21-cohort meta-analysis gives a pooled prognostic AUC of about 0.74 for circulating calprotectin in acute infection and sepsis; single cohorts link it to hospital mortality independently of renal function and to sepsis-associated AKI; S100A8/A9 genes sit in the neutrophil granule signature of severe malaria. Effects are moderate and calprotectin did not beat clinical severity scores.
rows.notes: Canine calprotectin and canine S100A12 were purified from dog leukocytes and have analytically validated species-specific radioimmunoassays with reference intervals, so this is among the most readily testable F3 gaps. S100A9 was not detected as a DS07 master protein, so the heterodimer cannot be confirmed from the public file alone.

rows.mechanism: Band neutrophilia and the neutrophil left shift as a cheap severity marker already in the haematology record
rows.human_direction: higher in severe disease: granulopoiesis and immature-neutrophil transcripts best explain severity in Gambian severe malaria, neutrophilia raises the odds of acute lung injury in knowlesi malaria
rows.notes: Added as a negative control for the family: the cheapest neutrophil marker has been tested against outcome in dogs with babesiosis, while every specific neutrophil-product marker has not.

rows.mechanism: VWF antigen, ultra-large multimers and ADAMTS13 (ratio)
rows.human_direction: VWF antigen, VWF activity and ultra-large multimers higher in severe and cerebral malaria; ADAMTS13 activity lower, so the VWF/ADAMTS13 ratio is higher in severe disease
rows.notes: Canine VWF:Ag ELISAs are standard in von Willebrand disease testing; the validation (Can J Vet Res 2008, PMC2568046) has no DOI. ADAMTS13 has never been measured in canine babesiosis. In the one canine study, VWF fell (consumption?) where it rises in human malaria. The direction may differ between species.

rows.human_direction: plasma CXCL4/PF4 higher in fatal cerebral malaria (one small Ghanaian cohort, 12 deaths); soluble P-selectin only a non-significant trend with 30-day mortality in 313 SIRS patients; PF4 drives experimental cerebral malaria in mice
rows.notes: Gap 'no' only because cell-surface CD62P was compared by outcome (CB504, CH03, 7 deaths). Soluble P-selectin and PF4/CXCL4 have never been measured in canine babesiosis, and no canine validation of a soluble assay was found. Human evidence is thin (grade 1).

rows.human_direction: PAI-1 higher in non-survivors and in more severe sepsis (meta-analysis of 18 studies, 4467 patients); PAI-1 high and tPA low in falciparum malaria
rows.cb_confirmed: CB004 (severity); CB145 (severity); CB439; CB034; CB476; CB019
rows.ds07_master: F1Q421 PLG (28%); E2R4V3 SERPINF2 (26%); Q6JDI3 PLG (17%)
rows.notes: Canine-specific PAI-1 ELISA (CB004) and chromogenic alpha-2-AP activity (CB145) used. Directions conflict with the human 'shutdown' picture: in B. canis, PAI-1 is low at admission; in B. rossi, alpha-2-AP is high only in survivors. tPA-modified TEG has not been used in babesiosis.

rows.mechanism: Protein C, antithrombin and thrombomodulin (anticoagulant failure)
rows.human_direction: low antithrombin and protein C activity with higher mortality, organ failure and DIC in sepsis; protein C, protein S and AT low in falciparum malaria; DIC goes with severe human babesiosis
rows.cb_confirmed: CB438 (severity); CB145 (severity); CB004 (severity); CB112 (severity); CB011; CB374; CB439; CB333; CB476
rows.notes: Well covered: 4 independent units (CB438, CB145/CH03, CB004, CB112) compared AT, protein C or TM by severity. Protein C (CB438, CB112) and AT (CB145) are lower in severe or fatal disease. In CB438 AT did not differ, so AT results are mixed.

rows.mechanism: Soluble endothelial protein C receptor (sEPCR) shedding
rows.human_direction: sEPCR higher in severe and cerebral malaria and in children who died (Benin); higher and rising in non-survivors of pneumococcal septic shock (278 patients)
rows.notes: Added because EPCR loss and shedding link coagulation to sequestration in falciparum malaria (PfEMP1 binds EPCR). No Babesia ligand for EPCR is known, so the transfer rests on sepsis-type shedding rather than parasite binding. The two Benin papers may share a cohort, so they are counted as one. 'Validated' rests on a canine-specific kit (CB011), not on a formal validation study.

rows.human_direction: mixed: raised by inflammation (higher in sepsis/septic shock; the hepcidin:ferritin ratio predicted septic-shock death, n=29), but suppressed in severe malarial anaemia compared with cerebral malaria (Kenyan children), so the direction depends on the phenotype
rows.notes: The canine severity evidence is one unit only: a small single-centre cohort from a non-PubMed journal, with a cut-off derived in the same sample, a generic Chinese ELISA rather than the LC-MS/MS reference method, and mortality that depended strongly on species (mixed infections about 92%). The PubMed canine babesiosis search returned 0 records. A replication with LC-MS/MS in B. rossi or B. canis would add a lot of value, even though the rule-based gap is 'no'.

rows.human_direction: higher in fatal sepsis/septic shock (MIMIC-IV n=718, OR 1.97 above 526 ng/mL; paediatric cohorts n=115 and n=123; septic shock n=79, https://doi.org/10.7759/cureus.115711); in malaria, ferritin is much higher in clinical than in asymptomatic infection (meta-analysis), but it is not independent of SOFA in some cohorts
rows.notes: The 'validated' grade rests on a canine-specific ferritin immunoassay with published canine use in leishmaniosis, cardiac disease and fracture studies. This PubMed pass found no formal method-validation paper. CB132 raises haemophagocytosis/hyperferritinaemia as a lead for severe disease, which parallels human hyperinflammation.

rows.human_direction: lower transferrin goes with death in sepsis (burn sepsis n=943, univariable). Higher, not lower, serum iron independently predicted 60-day death in septic ICU patients (n=133), so hypoferraemia itself is not a consistent severity marker in humans
rows.cb_confirmed: CB202 (severity); CB286 (severity); CB141 (severity); CB073 (severity); CB112 (severity); CB148; CB089; CB117; CB177; CB214; CB242; CB353; CB295
rows.ds07_master: E2QZQ1 TF (33%); J9P430 TF (23%); F1PEN6 TFRC (8%)
rows.notes: Serum iron and TIBC are generic colourimetric chemistry run on standard analysers (Roche Cobas in CH12), so the grade is used_in_dogs rather than a formal canine validation. Units: CH08 (CB202+CB286), CH12 (CB141), CH07 (CB073), CB112. The canine direction (lower iron and lower transferrin with severity) matches inflammatory hypoferraemia. Human sepsis data are inconsistent on serum iron. Transferrin saturation was never tested against severity in dogs.

rows.human_direction: higher basal cortisol in non-survivors (sepsis); adrenal androgens and ratios mostly not independent
rows.cb_confirmed: CB040 (severity); CB338 (severity); CB352 (severity); CB342 (severity); CB105 (severity); CB486 (severity); CB083; CB037
rows.notes: 5 units: CB040, CH31 (CB338+CB352), CB342, CH09 (CB105), CB486 (B. canis). 4 of 5 are Onderstepoort B. rossi; CB040 (2006-2016 patients) and CB342 (2007) may share patients with CH31, which cohorts.json does not resolve. Untested parts: adrenal androgens (never measured) and the cortisol:ACTH ratio (tested once by outcome, CB352, null). Assay graded validated as standard canine clinical endocrine immunoassays; no separate validation DOI retrieved.

rows.human_direction: lower T3 and T4 in non-survivors (sepsis meta-analysis of 8 studies, 1578 patients); TSH not different
rows.cb_confirmed: CB040 (severity); CB338 (severity); CB342 (severity); CB105 (severity); CB441 (severity); CB503; CB204
rows.notes: 5 units: CB040, CH31, CB342, CH09 (all Onderstepoort B. rossi, possible patient overlap as for F6-01) and CH35 (Warsaw B. canis). CH37 adds a within-infected correlation with azotaemia. T3 is the least tested by outcome. TTR in DS07 is an indirect proxy that can be tested now.

rows.human_direction: higher lactate in severe and fatal falciparum malaria (meta-analysis of 30 studies); hypoglycaemia and hyperlactataemia carry the highest case fatality
rows.cb_confirmed: CB040 (severity); CB516 (severity); CB263 (severity); CB074 (severity); CB486 (severity); CB537 (severity); CB394 (severity); CB112 (severity); CB342; CB340
rows.notes: 8 units with a severity or outcome contrast: CB040, CH21, CH18, CH08, CB486, CB537, CH33, CB112 (CB112 circular). Lactate alone: 4 units (CB040, CH21, CH18, CH08) in B. rossi, B. canis and B. gibsoni, all higher with death. Pre-2006 Onderstepoort lactate and hypoglycaemia studies are outside the review window and not counted.

rows.human_direction: higher IDO activity (kynurenine:tryptophan) and kynurenine with sepsis severity and death; CSF kynurenine and kynurenic acid with longer coma in cerebral malaria; kynurenine is vasodilatory and lowers blood pressure in murine malaria
rows.notes: Gap confirmed: one PubMed hit for dog babesiosis (CB091, infected vs healthy). Canine LC-MS/MS method for kynurenine and tryptophan validated (2026); IDO activity raised in canine pyometra. The vasodilatory role (10.1038/nm.2092) fits B. rossi hypotension. Not covered by HU001-HU027.

rows.human_direction: higher copeptin in sepsis non-survivors (two meta-analyses); in imported malaria copeptin is only a weak marker of severity (AUC 0.66, n=204) or not related to it
rows.notes: Gap confirmed: no dog babesiosis study measured copeptin or AVP (CB044 suspected SIADH without measuring it). Assay caveat: serum copeptin tracked osmotic stimulation in Beagles (10.1111/jvim.70219), but an ELISA agreed poorly with ADH in cardiac dogs (10.3390/ani15071013), so graded used_in_dogs, not validated. Human malaria evidence is weak; the grade rests on sepsis.

rows.human_direction: IL-10 and TNF both higher in severe and fatal malaria; a low IL-10/TNF ratio (inadequate IL-10 for the TNF level) goes with severe disease
rows.cb_confirmed: CB517 (severity); CB050 (severity); CB037 (severity); CB017 (severity); CB109 (severity); CB473 (severity); CB098; CB101; CB075; CB298
rows.notes: Units: CH03, CB037, CH23, CB109 (mRNA), CH37 (TNF correlations only). Only CB037 measured both IL-10 and TNF in one severity contrast; no dog study reported the IL-10/TNF ratio, so the ratio is a narrow sub-gap that DS02 can address descriptively. Results mixed: IL-10 raised by infection but not by outcome in CH03 or CH23 (SV-04).

rows.mechanism: Regulatory T cells and T-cell exhaustion (PD-1, PD-L1)
rows.human_direction: Tregs expanded in severe malaria in proportion to parasite burden; higher PD-1 / PD-L1 on T cells and antigen-presenting cells goes with organ dysfunction, secondary infection and death in sepsis
rows.notes: PubMed returned 0 dog babesiosis studies. Canine Treg flow (CD4+CD25+FoxP3+) and PD-1/PD-L1 used in canine sepsis model and leishmaniasis with cross-reactive or canine antibodies, without formal validation.

rows.mechanism: Monocyte deactivation (HLA-DR / DLA class II expression)
rows.human_direction: low and persistently low monocyte HLA-DR goes with death and secondary infection in septic shock; monocyte activation markers including HLA-DR altered in children with malaria
rows.notes: Measured_no_severity rests only on transcript-level data (CB082). No canine monocyte DLA-DR flow study in babesiosis or by outcome found; canine CD14+ MHCII flow exists (haematological disorders, leishmaniasis).

rows.human_direction: higher suPAR and sTREM-1 in severe malaria and in those who die; suPAR prognostic in sepsis (meta-analysis)
rows.notes: Status is driven by suPAR (one unit, B. canis, null). sTREM-1 has never been measured in dogs with babesiosis and no canine soluble TREM-1 assay was found; it is split out as F7-11. A B. rossi suPAR by outcome study does not exist.

rows.human_direction: higher presepsin (sCD14-ST) predicts death in sepsis (meta-analyses); no malaria severity cohort found
rows.notes: Only measured by untargeted proteomics (total CD14, not the presepsin fragment); no canine sCD14 or presepsin immunoassay found in PubMed. Part b re-tests the same DS07 data, so it is not independent confirmation.

rows.human_direction: higher sTREM-1 in severe malaria and best single predictor of death in African children with severe malaria
rows.notes: Canine evidence is TREM-1 expression and function on canine neutrophils only; no canine soluble TREM-1 immunoassay found, so a serum test would need a cross-reactive kit to be validated first.

rows.human_direction: higher plasma factor H in severe than uncomplicated falciparum malaria (149 Gambian children) and linked to higher parasite multiplication rate; parasite blood stages bind factor H to evade complement
rows.notes: Measured in dogs only by mass spectrometry; no canine factor H immunoassay found. CB112's global test implicitly covered factor H but reported nothing, so an explicit DS07 test (part b) would be the first severity contrast. Human evidence comes from one Gambian group (two papers, overlapping children) plus a Ghanaian FHR-1 genetic cohort.

sections.heading: Question
paragraphs: Which mechanisms linked to severity in malaria, human babesiosis and sepsis have not been measured against severity in dogs with babesiosis, have a canine assay, and could be tested now? Premise: most mechanisms with good human evidence are unmeasured in dogs.

sections.heading: What was done
paragraphs: Seven sub-agents, one per mechanism family, graded 37 mechanisms (29 seeds fixed in the spec, 8 added by agents) on the human evidence (HU comparator notes, then targeted PubMed searches), the canine evidence (a keyword search of the 444 CB notes and 503 CB texts, of which 234 are full texts, read and confirmed by the agent, then PubMed), the canine assay, and whether a public file holds the protein or gene. Gap, testability and rank were then recomputed by a script from the rules of the spec.
Ranking rule: a gap, human grade 2 or more, and a canine assay; then ordered by human grade, assay, test-now and the number of canine studies. At most 10.

sections.heading: Result
paragraphs: 21 of 37 mechanisms are gaps: 12 were never measured in dogs with babesiosis and 9 were measured only against controls or over time. 16 have canine severity data.
Of 36 mechanisms with human grade 2 or 3, 21 are gaps (58%), so the premise holds. Of the 26 grade-3 mechanisms, 10 already have canine severity data.

21 mechanisms meet the ranking rule; the top 10: 1. Angiopoietin-2 and the Ang-2/Ang-1 ratio; 2. VEGF and soluble VEGFR-1; 3. Neutrophil extracellular traps (cell-free DNA, MPO-DNA, citrullinated histone H3); 4. Circulating extracellular histones (host and parasite); 5. Calprotectin (S100A8/A9) and S100A12 as circulating neutrophil activation alarmins; 6. VWF antigen, ultra-large multimers and ADAMTS13 (ratio); 7. Ferritin (hyperferritinaemia); 8. Kynurenine pathway (IDO, kynurenine, quinolinic acid); 9. Released (plasma) myeloperoxidase and neutrophil elastase, as degranulation markers distinct from the cellular MPXI; 10. Haem oxygenase-1 induction. Eligible but below the cut of 10: Glycocalyx shedding (syndecan-1, heparan sulfate, hyaluronan); Regulatory T cells and T-cell exhaustion (PD-1, PD-L1); Soluble TREM-1 (split from F7-04); Cell-free (plasma) haemoglobin; Monocyte deactivation (HLA-DR / DLA class II expression); Copeptin / vasopressin; Soluble endothelial protein C receptor (sEPCR) shedding; Haptoglobin depletion; ADMA and arginine bioavailability (plasma arginine:ADMA ratio); Free haem and haemopexin depletion; Complement regulation (complement factor H).

2 ranked mechanisms have a master protein in the DS07 serum proteome (complicated against uncomplicated B. rossi), so part b can look at them now: Circulating extracellular histones (host and parasite); Calprotectin (S100A8/A9) and S100A12 as circulating neutrophil activation alarmins. The other 8 have no circulating-protein measure in any public file (at most DS06 blood RNA) and need stored samples and a canine assay.
Sensitivity (post hoc): if DS06 blood RNA does not count as testable now, the top 10 gains Cell-free (plasma) haemoglobin and loses Haem oxygenase-1 induction.
Every gap with strong human evidence has some canine assay.

sections.heading: What this does not show
paragraphs: A gap means not found in PubMed and in the local corpus on 2026-11-12; about half the CB texts are abstracts only, and one database was searched. Grades are agent judgements recorded with their DOIs; no human reviewed them.

Human evidence does not transfer by itself: B. rossi, B. canis and B. gibsoni differ from P. falciparum (no cytoadherence of the same kind is established), and sepsis is a different disease. The list says what to measure, not what will be found.

A DS06 gene is expression in the blood of 5 experimental Beagles, not circulating protein, and that file has no severity contrast beyond one death. DS07 has a severity label but 14 against 18 dogs and no clinical values; proteins that follow anaemia (haemoglobin, haptoglobin) partly restate the label. No test was run here.
